subject: treehouse
pitch: A cozy treehouse diorama on a grassy round base. A thick old oak with a wide leafy crown, a little wooden cabin with a red shingle roof and a round window nestled in its branches, a rope ladder and a wooden swing hanging below, a pennant flag on the roof, a lantern by the door, and a few mushrooms and a bicycle at the foot of the tree.
reasoning:
I need to write a single TypeScript module using the SDK, but its API is only partially documented, so I should be careful to use only the builder methods I know exist—things like joint, chain, and sweep with their documented options.

To stay safe, I'll stick to simpler, well-understood constructs: joints, parts, rods/capsules, sweeps with path arrays, and sticks, avoiding the riskier or underspecified functions. I'll skip random number generation entirely and rely on deterministic arithmetic instead, then plan the actual diorama scene—a round grassy base, an oak trunk, a leafy crown built from clustered spheres, and a small cabin nestled in the branches with a red shingle roof.

For the roof itself I'm considering a pyramidal cone or a slanted box, aiming cylindrical pieces using the `dir` option on parts rather than any lookAt-style rotation, assuming it orients the geometry's Y-axis along the given direction. Since joints are limited and mostly unnecessary for a static diorama, I'll keep the skeleton minimal—just a root trunk joint—and treat most props as plain geometry attached directly without extra bones.

For scale, I'm roughing out real-world proportions: a roughly 12m oak-sized tree, a 3m-wide cabin, and a diorama base disc around 6m in radius, with the trunk height scaled to match.

Working through the base disc's dimensions so it sits flush or sinks only slightly below the floor line — aiming for a thin disc centered near y=0.1 so its lowest point barely touches zero while staying within the allowed sink tolerance relative to the model's total height.

I'm also planning the layered base: an earth-brown cylinder topped with a thinner green grass disc, then sketching the tree's components — a tapered trunk cylinder, angled branch cylinders using direction vectors, and a crown built from clustered low-poly icosahedrons positioned to look like foliage, with the cabin nestled among the upper branches.

Now I'm working out the cabin structure itself: a flat platform box resting on a branch fork, box walls above it, and for the roof I'm considering how to fake a pyramid or gable shape since the builder doesn't directly support rotated cone geometry, so I'll likely construct a custom triangular prism BufferGeometry from raw vertices to get the gable look.

I'm orienting the gable so its ridge runs along Z, which puts the triangular ends facing front and back where the door and window sit, with the roof sloping down toward the sides—figuring out the cross-section triangle coordinates and overhang width for the eaves.

For color, I want the sloped roof panels red but the gable triangles a wood tone, so I'll keep them as separate geometries rather than one shared-color mesh. I'm also working out winding order for each quad and triangle so the faces render correctly from outside, computing normals against an outward hint point and flipping vertices when needed to avoid invisible backfaces.

Now I'm planning the cabin details: a circular window using a thin cylinder for the glass and a torus for the frame (conveniently oriented in the XY plane facing forward by default), plus a front door box and wall dimensions, working out vertical positions so the deck, wall bottoms, cabin body, and roof eave all line up correctly.

I'm calculating the gable triangle geometry for the roof ends — figuring out how the ridge height, door, and round window positions relate to the eave line, and wrestling with whether to treat the gable as part of the extruded roof prism or a separate overhanging face, deciding to simplify by having the roof prism extend slightly beyond the wall depth.

I'll split the roof into two separate geometries: sloped quads for the two roof planes and triangles for the gable ends, both built from the same set of corner points so the overhang sits correctly at the front and back faces.

To get consistent winding without manual guesswork, I'm writing a generic helper that takes a triangle list plus an interior reference point, computes each face normal, and flips vertices if the normal points toward the hint instead of away from it—this way every custom shape in the scene can reuse the same orientation-fixing logic.

Now I'm thinking through the oak tree construction: a tapered trunk cylinder, forked branches built from a limb helper that computes midpoint/direction/length between two points, and a leafy crown made of overlapping icosahedron blobs in two shades of green, all arranged so a branch can support the treehouse platform near the crown's base.

I'm placing roughly ten faceted icosahedron blobs at varied positions and sizes around the trunk to form a layered canopy that partially surrounds and overlaps the cabin, leaving part of it visible while looking naturally nestled among the foliage.

Now I'm repositioning the front-facing blobs so they don't block the cabin door, shifting them deeper or farther sideways while keeping the crown wide and bushy overhead and to the sides. I'm also recalculating the cabin's position and dimensions—centering it slightly off-trunk, defining wall spans, roof overhang, and a supporting deck platform sized to match the walls beneath it.

I'm adding a couple of small branch supports connecting the trunk to the deck, then designing a hanging rope ladder from the deck's front-left edge down to the ground, with paired rope cylinders and evenly spaced horizontal rungs, angling it slightly outward as it descends.

For the swing, I'm planning a branch extending from the trunk higher up to serve as the mounting point, with two ropes dropping down to a seat board, making sure the rope positions align with the seat's ends for balanced hanging.

I'll build my own helper using part placement with midpoint and direction instead of relying on an unknown rod signature. Now I'm placing a thin pole at the roof ridge for a pennant flag.

Still planning flag geometry...

I'll make the pennant double-sided by adding reversed-winding duplicate triangles, colored red-orange. For the lantern by the door, I'm placing it on a small bracket post near the front-right of the deck.

Positioning it slightly right of the door at x=1.85, with a thin cylinder post holding up a small yellow box lantern topped with a pyramidal cap.

For mushrooms at the tree's base, I'll build stems from thin cylinders and caps using hemisphere spheres, clustering three of them near the trunk while avoiding the ladder's footprint. Then I'm sketching the bicycle on the opposite side of the tree, starting with two torus wheels.

Figuring out wheel orientation...

Decided: wheels as low-poly dark cylinders with light hubs, positioned near the tree's foot at roughly (1.8, 0.6, 3.0), with wheel centers offset along z by about ±0.55.

Now I'm laying out the bike frame geometry: thin rod tubes connecting rear hub, bottom bracket, seat post, head tube, and fork to front hub, all constrained to the x=1.8 plane for a proper side-view silhouette, plus a small seat box and cylindrical tires at each hub position.

For the base, I'm defining an earth cylinder (radius 7, height 0.5) topped by a grass layer reaching y=0.6, verifying the bicycle and tree trunk sit correctly at that ground level. The trunk runs from 0.6 up to 5.8, with a slightly flared base cylinder for root support, and now I'm starting to plan the branch limbs extending from the trunk top to support the treehouse deck.

Now I'm computing the geometry for the swing branch and crown branches, working out start/end points and radii for each limb, then parameterizing the swing branch to find exact rope attachment positions by lerping x, y, z coordinates for the two swing points and placing the seat board around y=3.6.

I'm now sizing the swing seat box and verifying the rope positions align with the seat ends, then turning to the ladder: setting up the vertical ropes hanging from the deck's front edge down to near ground level, and spacing out rungs every 0.45 units along the ladder's length.

Finally I'm placing the round gable window — figuring out where it sits on the sloped roof face using the gable's width-at-height formula so the torus frame fits comfortably within the triangular gable without clipping its edges.

I'm checking the wall and roof box dimensions line up correctly with the eave and ridge heights, then assigning colors: reddish roof, cream wood walls, darker cream gables, brown door, and a light blue glass window.

Now I'm picking colors for the remaining elements — glass window with torus frame, deck planks, tree bark and layered leaf greens, grass and earth tones, a red pennant, lantern glow, red-capped mushrooms with white dot spheres on top, pale stems, and a blue-framed bike with dark tires. I'm keeping the total palette under the flat-color limit, around 25 distinct colors, then moving on to building the mushroom caps as hemisphere geometries.

I'm working out exact positions so each mushroom's stem and cap stack correctly on top of each other and sit flush on the floor at y=0, placing a few varied-size mushrooms near each other, and double-checking that grass and earth meet the ground plane with no gap. I'm also reasoning through how the "at" placement parameter should interact with each geometry's local origin, making sure cylinders and spheres that are already centered work correctly, while custom triangle geometries built from absolute coordinates need to be anchored at the origin to behave consistently.

I realize I can make this robust either way by computing the bounding box center of each custom geometry, recentering the geometry on the origin, and passing that center as `at` — this satisfies both possible translation semantics. I'll build a helper that does this centering (computing bbox, translating by negative center, returning the center), making sure winding order is handled before centering occurs.

For the rig, a single root joint named "base" at the origin should suffice since this is a diorama rather than a creature, so every part can just attach to that one joint by default. For foliage, I'll use low-poly icosahedron blobs for the crown and scattered leaf clusters to add visual detail, plus a few hanging accents for extra texture.

Now I'm adding cabin details: a chimney box positioned on the roof slope with stone-grey coloring, a flagpole with a pennant triangle on the ridge, and glass windows with frames on the side and front walls to break up the plain surfaces.

Setting up types, vector math helpers, and a tapered-rod utility function for constructing the treehouse geometry...

Finishing the solid mesh builder, then setting up the roof geometry with sloped sides and gable triangles, computing hint centers to verify correct outward-facing normals.

For the canopy, I'm placing icosahedron blobs at leaf positions to form the foliage clusters, considering whether their default non-indexed normals will look sufficiently smooth or flat-shaded for this low-detail shape.

Now I'm working out the trunk and branch skeleton: a tapered cylinder rod for the trunk, then a set of branch rods (deck support, swing branch, right branch, upper-left branch, central top, and back upper-right) each defined by start/end points and tapering radii to build out the tree's structure.

I'm then sketching the cabin: a flat deck box sized and positioned to sit on the branch support, walls and gable boxes with wood and cream coloring, and a door box, while deciding to skip railing posts to avoid collisions with the ladder and keep the design simpler.

For the door and window, I'm fine-tuning exact z-offsets so the door and frame boxes don't overlap oddly, deciding to skip a separate door frame for simplicity, then placing a front window with a glass pane box and a slightly offset brown frame box behind it.

I'm now adding a side window on the +X wall with similar glass and frame boxes, nudging positions to avoid z-fighting, and considering whether to include it for visual interest since the deck extends out that far. For the gable, I'm placing a round window using a torus frame plus a cylindrical glass disk, positioning both just in front of the gable triangle face.

Next I'm working out the chimney as a stone-colored box with a slightly wider cap, positioned so its base sinks into the roof slope to look embedded. I add a flagpole rod at the ridge, then a flag made of two triangles (with reversed winding for double-sided visibility) extending off the pole. Finally I'm adding a lantern fixture near the porch: a dark post rod, a yellow box body, and a cone cap on top.

Now I'm placing the ladder on the side of the treehouse — two vertical rope cylinders running from the deck underside down near the ground, with roughly ten horizontal wooden rungs spaced at regular intervals, checking that the bottom ends land just above the grass without clipping through it.

Next I'm working out the swing: calculating an attachment function to interpolate points along the tilted branch, then positioning two diagonal ropes running down to a wooden seat box, adjusting rope endpoints so they meet cleanly at the top surface of the seat.

I'm designing a mushroom-generation function with a stem cylinder, a hemisphere cap, and small white spheres positioned on the cap surface as spots, checking that the spot placement math keeps them sitting just outside the cap radius. I'm now placing a few mushrooms at specific coordinates near the base.

Then I'm laying out a bicycle at x=1.8, defining key frame points (bottom bracket, seat, head tube, hubs) and connecting them with rods to form the top tube, down tube, seat stay, and fork, plus adding handlebar geometry at the head tube location.

I'm sizing a seat box above the seat post, then building the wheels as thin cylinders with small gray hub cylinders, oriented along the x-axis so they sit flush with the frame. I'm checking the wheel radius and ground clearance line up correctly, then confirming overall scale against real-world bike and tree dimensions before adding flaring roots at the trunk base and starting the leaf crown with a dark color scheme.

Now I'm placing individual leaf-blob spheres around the crown with varying colors and radii, checking that none overlap the cabin or the ladder, and adjusting one blob's position so it doesn't collide with the pennant pole near the top of the tree.

The deck support branch runs from the trunk into the deck's underside, acting as structural support. Overall part count lands around 120, which seems reasonable, and I'm doing a final bounds check to confirm the crown top sits near 12.1 before finalizing the builder call.

I'll add a single root joint at the base so parts without an explicit bone attachment default to it, satisfying the "exactly one root joint" requirement. Now writing the final TypeScript module with imports, metadata, vector helper functions, and color constants for the scene...

Writing geometry helper code...

Writing mushroom helper function...

I normalize those spot directions and position them on the hemisphere cap, then move on to assembling the rest of the scene: the lantern, bike frame, crown blobs, and leaf list with color mappings, finishing up with the base cylinder geometry.

Now I'm layering the ground details—earth and grass cylinders stacked with slightly different radii, plus scattered grass tufts and flower cones placed deterministically around the base at alternating angles. I'm also working out the swing attachment points, interpolating between two anchor positions to place the rope and seat correctly.

Verifying the seat width and rope endpoints align so the ropes attach cleanly at the seat edges, then finalizing the code with a brief explanatory note.
